P.title: P.blurb
World: The planet and its people: seasons, time zones, languages and cities.

P.title: wo-planet.summary
World: Seasons, time zones, coordinates and the ocean's central heating.

P.title: wo-planet.q0.x
World: The 23.4° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.

P.title: wo-planet.q1.q
World: Two places are 45° of longitude apart. Roughly how many hours apart are their clocks?

P.title: wo-planet.q2.x
World: Latitude runs from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles.

P.title: wo-planet.q3.q
World: Why does the Sun rise in the east?

P.title: wo-planet.q3.o1
World: Earth spins from west to east

P.title: wo-planet.q3.x
World: Rotation makes the Sun appear to move.

P.title: wo-planet.q4.q
World: About how fast do tectonic plates move?

P.title: wo-planet.q4.x
World: Roughly as fast as fingernails grow.

P.title: wo-planet.c0.text
World: It isn't about distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of our winter.\n\nSeasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4°. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer. In December it leans away.

P.title: wo-planet.c1.text
World: Earth turns 360° a day, so each hour of time difference is about 15° of longitude. Countries round that off to suit their borders, and a few, like India, use half hours. Move Lisbon's clock (winter time) and watch the world follow.

P.title: wo-planet.c2.text
World: Every place on Earth has two coordinates. Latitude says how far north or south of the equator you are, from 0° to 90°. Longitude says how far east or west of the Greenwich meridian in London, from 0° to 180°.\n\nViana do Castelo sits at about 41.7° N, 8.8° W.

P.title: wo-planet.c3.text
World: Porto and New York sit at almost the same latitude, yet Porto's winters are far milder. Part of the reason is the Gulf Stream and its extension, which carry warm tropical water north-east across the Atlantic.\n\nWesterly winds blowing off that warm ocean bring the heat ashore. Cold water returns south, completing a vast loop.

P.title: wo-planet.c4.text
World: Earth spins once on its axis about every 24 hours, from west to east. That's why the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and why Japan sees sunrise hours before Portugal.

P.title: wo-planet.c4.viz.steps.1
World: Sun appears to rise in the east

P.title: wo-planet.c5.text
World: Somewhere the calendar must change day. The date line runs roughly along 180° longitude through the Pacific; crossing it westward you jump a day ahead.

P.title: wo-planet.c6.text
World: Around 21 June, the northern hemisphere has its longest day (summer solstice); around 21 December its shortest. At the equinoxes in March and September, day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

P.title: wo-planet.c7.text
World: In Lisbon, the longest day has about 14 h 50 min of daylight and the shortest about 9 h 30 min. Near the poles, summer brings the midnight sun.

P.title: wo-planet.c8.text
World: Beneath the thin crust lies the hot mantle, then a liquid outer core and a solid inner core about as hot as the Sun's surface.

P.title: wo-planet.c9.text
World: Earth's crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Where they meet, we get earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

P.title: wo-people.summary
World: Who lives where, what they speak, and why cities are where they are.

P.title: wo-people.q0.q
World: Which region is home to most of the world's people?

P.title: wo-people.q0.x
World: Roughly 59 out of every 100 people live in Asia.

P.title: wo-people.q1.q
World: Which language has the most native speakers?

P.title: wo-people.q1.x
World: Mandarin leads on native speakers; English leads when learners are included.

P.title: wo-people.q2.q
World: Why did so many big cities grow on rivers and coasts?

P.title: wo-people.q2.o1
World: Water, food and cheap transport for trade

P.title: wo-people.q2.o2
World: Easier to defend from the air

P.title: wo-people.q2.x
World: Water routes were the cheapest way to move goods and people for most of history.

P.title: wo-people.q3.q
World: Which country became the most populous in 2023?

P.title: wo-people.q4.x
World: The UN marked it in November 2022.

P.title: wo-people.c0.text
World: About 8 billion people live on Earth; the UN marked the milestone in November 2022. Shrink that to 100 people and roughly 59 live in Asia, 18 in Africa, 9 in Europe, 8 in Latin America, 5 in North America and 1 in Oceania.\n\nIndia and China alone hold more than a third of humanity. Africa is the fastest-growing region.

P.title: wo-people.c1.text
World: Count everyone who speaks a language, natives and learners together, and English comes first, with Mandarin Chinese second. Count only native speakers and Mandarin leads by a long way.\n\nPortuguese has around 260 million speakers worldwide, most of them in Brazil, which makes it the most spoken language in the southern hemisphere.

P.title: wo-people.c2.title
World: Why cities sit on rivers and coasts

P.title: wo-people.c2.text
World: Before railways and roads, water was the motorway. Rivers and sheltered harbours offered drinking water, fertile soil, fish and, above all, cheap transport for trade.\n\nThat's why so many great cities stand at a river mouth or a natural harbour: Lisbon on the Tagus, Porto on the Douro, London on the Thames, Shanghai at the mouth of the Yangtze.

P.title: wo-people.c3.text
World: The usual answer is 195: the 193 members of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican City and Palestine. Some places, like Taiwan and Kosovo, govern themselves but aren't UN members, so counts differ.\n\nThe largest is Russia, at about 17 million km². The smallest, Vatican City, is under half a square kilometre.

P.title: wo-people.c4.text
World: World population took until about 1800 to reach 1 billion, then grew rapidly with better medicine and food: 2 billion in 1927, 4 billion in 1974, 8 billion in 2022.

P.title: wo-people.c5.text
World: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023, each with about 1.4 billion people. Then come the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan.

P.title: wo-people.c6.text
World: Many rich countries, including Portugal, Italy and Japan, have low birth rates and long lives, so populations are ageing. Portugal has one of the oldest populations in Europe.

P.title: wo-people.c7.text
World: Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900, from about 32 years to over 70. Portugal's is around 81 years.

P.title: wo-people.c8.text
World: About 280 million people live outside the country where they were born, around 3.5% of humanity. Portugal has been a country of emigration and, more recently, of immigration too.

P.title: wo-people.c9.text
World: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries on four continents, from Brazil to Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde and Timor-Leste. Millions more Portuguese descendants live in France, the USA, Canada, Brazil and Switzerland.

P.title: wo-people.c9.viz.items.3
World: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe

P.title: wo-continents.summary
World: The big pieces of the world map.

P.title: wo-continents.q1.o1
World: A supercontinent joining all the land

P.title: wo-continents.q1.x
World: It broke apart over millions of years.

P.title: wo-continents.q2.q
World: What share of Earth's surface is ocean?

P.title: wo-continents.q2.x
World: Most of the planet is water.

P.title: wo-continents.c0.text
World: The usual list is Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia/Oceania. Some countries count the Americas as one continent, or Europe and Asia as Eurasia.

P.title: wo-continents.c1.text
World: The Pacific is the biggest, larger than all the land combined. Then come the Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

P.title: wo-continents.c2.text
World: About 71% of Earth's surface is ocean. Most fresh water is locked in ice; less than 1% of all water is fresh and easy to reach.

P.title: wo-continents.c3.text
World: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, in the Pacific, is about 11 km deep, deeper than Everest is high.

P.title: wo-continents.c4.text
World: About 300 million years ago, the continents were joined in a supercontinent called Pangaea. It broke apart slowly; South America and Africa still fit together like puzzle pieces.

P.title: wo-continents.c5.text
World: Europe and Asia share one landmass. By convention the boundary follows the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, which means Russia and Turkey span both.

P.title: wo-continents.c6.text
World: Greenland is the world's largest island. Portugal's Atlantic islands, Madeira and the Azores, are volcanic; the Azores sit where three tectonic plates meet.

P.title: wo-continents.c7.text
World: Ocean currents act like conveyor belts, carrying heat around the planet. The Gulf Stream warms western Europe; the cold Canary Current runs down Portugal's coast, keeping summer seas cool.

P.title: wo-continents.c8.text
World: Narrow straits are vital shipping lanes: Gibraltar (Atlantic–Mediterranean), Suez Canal (Mediterranean–Red Sea), Hormuz (Persian Gulf), Malacca (Indian Ocean–Pacific), Panama Canal.

P.title: wo-continents.c9.text
World: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent, covered by ice up to 4.8 km thick. It holds about 70% of the world's fresh water. No country owns it; the 1959 Antarctic Treaty reserves it for science.

P.title: wo-climate.summary
World: Why deserts, rainforests and tundra are where they are.

P.title: wo-climate.q0.q
World: Most of Portugal has which climate?

P.title: wo-climate.q0.x
World: Hot dry summers, mild wet winters.

P.title: wo-climate.q1.q
World: Roughly how much does temperature drop per 1,000 m of altitude?

P.title: wo-climate.q2.o1
World: Mountains forcing air up so rain falls on one side

P.title: wo-climate.c0.text
World: Weather is what happens today; climate is the average pattern over decades. "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get."

P.title: wo-climate.c1.text
World: Near the equator the Sun is high all year, so it's hot. Towards the poles, sunlight arrives at a low angle and is spread out, so it's cold.

P.title: wo-climate.c2.text
World: The Köppen system classifies climates by temperature and rainfall. Most of Portugal has a Mediterranean climate (Csa/Csb): hot or warm dry summers and mild wet winters.

P.title: wo-climate.c3.text
World: Deserts get less than about 250 mm of rain a year. Many lie around 30° latitude, where dry air sinks. The Sahara is the largest hot desert; Antarctica is technically the largest desert of all.

P.title: wo-climate.c4.text
World: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator with heat and rain all year. They cover about 6% of the land but hold over half of all species. The Amazon is the largest.

P.title: wo-climate.c5.text
World: A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants and animals: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, Mediterranean scrub, temperate forest, taiga, tundra, grassland.

P.title: wo-climate.c6.text
World: Temperature drops about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m of altitude. Serra da Estrela can be snowy while Lisbon is mild. Mountains also force air up, making one side wet and the other dry (rain shadow).

P.title: wo-climate.c7.text
World: In South Asia, summer winds reverse and blow in from the warm ocean, bringing months of heavy rain. Over a billion people depend on the monsoon for farming.

P.title: wo-climate.c8.text
World: The northwest (Minho) is one of Europe's rainiest regions; the interior Alentejo is hot and dry, often over 40 °C in summer. The Atlantic coast is mild; the interior has bigger temperature swings.

P.title: wo-climate.c9.text
World: Cities are warmer than the countryside (urban heat islands); valleys collect cold air at night; coasts are milder. Vineyards and gardens exploit these small differences.

P.title: wo-rivers.summary
World: The world's great rivers and ranges.

P.title: wo-rivers.q0.q
World: Which river carries the most water?

P.title: wo-rivers.q0.x
World: About a fifth of world river discharge.

P.title: wo-rivers.q2.o1
World: The Indian plate colliding with Asia

P.title: wo-rivers.c0.text
World: The Nile and the Amazon compete for the title of longest river, each around 6,400–7,000 km depending on how it's measured. The Amazon carries by far the most water.

P.title: wo-rivers.c1.text
World: The Amazon discharges about 20% of all river water entering the oceans, more than the next seven largest rivers combined.

P.title: wo-rivers.c2.text
World: The first civilisations grew along rivers: the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus and the Yellow River, with water, fertile soil and transport.

P.title: wo-rivers.c3.text
World: The Tejo (Tagus) is the longest river in Iberia, rising in Spain and reaching the sea at Lisbon. The Douro, Guadiana and Minho also start in Spain; the Mondego is the longest entirely Portuguese river.

P.title: wo-rivers.c4.text
World: All fourteen peaks over 8,000 m are in the Himalaya and Karakoram in Asia. Everest, at 8,849 m, is the highest above sea level.

P.title: wo-rivers.c5.text
World: Portugal's highest point is Mount Pico in the Azores, a volcano of 2,351 m. On the mainland, the highest is Torre in the Serra da Estrela, at 1,993 m.

P.title: wo-rivers.c6.text
World: Most great ranges form where tectonic plates collide and crumple: the Himalaya (India hitting Asia), the Alps (Africa pushing into Europe). Others are volcanic, like the Andes' peaks.

P.title: wo-rivers.c7.text
World: Glaciers are rivers of ice that carve U-shaped valleys and fjords. They store fresh water but are shrinking almost everywhere as the climate warms.

P.title: wo-rivers.c8.text
World: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area; Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest and oldest, holding about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.

P.title: wo-rivers.c9.text
World: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall (979 m). Victoria Falls and Iguaçu are among the widest and most spectacular.

P.title: wo-europe.summary
World: A small continent with many countries and languages.

P.title: wo-europe.q0.q
World: How many countries are in the EU?

P.title: wo-europe.c0.text
World: Europe has about 44–50 countries depending on how you count, with around 745 million people, on just 7% of the world's land.

P.title: wo-europe.c1.text
World: The EU has 27 member states that share a single market, free movement of people and many common laws. 21 of them use the euro; Bulgaria was the latest to join, in 2026.

P.title: wo-europe.c2.text
World: In the Schengen area, people cross borders without passport checks. It includes most EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

P.title: wo-europe.c3.text
World: The EU has 24 official languages. Most European languages belong to the Indo-European family: Romance (Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian), Germanic (English, German, Dutch) and Slavic (Polish, Czech).

P.title: wo-europe.c4.text
World: Basque (Euskara), spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France, is unrelated to any other known language, probably older than the Indo-European languages around it.

P.title: wo-europe.c5.text
World: Germany is Europe's largest economy, followed by the UK and France. Portugal's economy is mid-sized, with tourism, services, exports and manufacturing.

P.title: wo-europe.c6.text
World: Europe has tiny countries: Vatican City (0.44 km²), Monaco, San Marino, Liechtenstein and Andorra, which borders Spain and France high in the Pyrenees.

P.title: wo-europe.c7.text
World: The Volga is Europe's longest river; the Danube flows through ten countries. The Alps are the highest range, with Mont Blanc at 4,806 m.

P.title: wo-europe.c8.text
World: Portugal and Spain share the Iberian Peninsula, with Andorra and Gibraltar (British). The peninsula is separated from Africa by the 14 km Strait of Gibraltar.

P.title: wo-europe.c8.viz.items.0.l
World: Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest

P.title: wo-europe.c9.text
World: Europe's regions differ in climate, economy and history: Nordic welfare states, the industrial centre, the Mediterranean south, and former communist countries in the east.

P.title: wo-poles.summary
World: Ice sheets and sea ice, who owns the poles, polar peoples, research and a melting future.

P.title: wo-poles.q0.q
World: What is an iceberg made of?

P.title: wo-poles.q0.x
World: Icebergs break off glaciers and ice shelves formed from snow.

P.title: wo-poles.q1.q
World: What did the Antarctic Treaty do with territorial claims?

P.title: wo-poles.q1.x
World: Claims are frozen, and no new ones can be made.

P.title: wo-poles.q2.q
World: When is Arctic sea ice at its smallest?

P.title: wo-poles.q2.x
World: It melts through the summer and reaches its minimum in September.

P.title: wo-poles.q3.o1
World: Melting land ice and warming water

P.title: wo-poles.q3.o2
World: More rain falling on the sea

P.title: wo-poles.q3.x
World: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of water.

P.title: wo-poles.c0.text
World: Polar ice comes in different kinds. Ice sheets are vast domes of compacted snow on land, kilometres thick; today only Greenland and Antarctica have them.\n\nSea ice is frozen seawater, usually only a few metres thick. Ice shelves are the floating edges of ice sheets, and icebergs break off from them.

P.title: wo-poles.c1.text
World: Sea ice grows and shrinks with the seasons. Arctic ice peaks in March and is smallest in September; Antarctic ice does the opposite.\n\nEach winter the sea around Antarctica freezes over an area larger than the continent itself, then most of it melts again. This yearly pulse is one of the biggest seasonal changes on Earth.

P.title: wo-poles.c2.text
World: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and three of the claims overlap. Most other countries, including Portugal, do not recognise any claim.\n\nThe Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959, puts these claims on hold. Antarctica is the only continent where no country exercises full sovereignty.

P.title: wo-poles.c3.text
World: Unlike Antarctica, the Arctic has no special treaty. Its lands belong to eight countries, and its ocean is governed by the international law of the sea.\n\nEach coastal state controls fishing and resources up to 200 nautical miles out. Several are asking to extend their seabed rights all the way to the North Pole.

P.title: wo-poles.c4.text
World: About four million people live in the Arctic, in towns, mining cities and small villages. Around one in ten belongs to an Indigenous people, such as the Inuit, Sámi, Nenets or Chukchi.\n\nMany Arctic communities now govern themselves, combining modern life with hunting, herding and their own languages.

P.title: wo-poles.c5.text
World: The two polar regions take turns. When the Arctic has its midnight sun in June, Antarctica is deep in polar night, and six months later they swap.\n\nLong twilights soften the change, and in the dark months auroras often light up the sky near both poles.

P.title: wo-poles.c6.text
World: About 30 countries run around 70 research stations in Antarctica. In summer several thousand people live there; in winter about a thousand stay.\n\nIn the Arctic, scientists work in towns and remote camps, from the international village of Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard to stations in Greenland, Canada and Alaska.

P.title: wo-poles.c7.text
World: Snow falling on ice sheets traps tiny bubbles of air. Layer by layer it builds an archive of the atmosphere going back hundreds of thousands of years.\n\nBy drilling cores kilometres long, scientists can read past temperatures and greenhouse gas levels, and show how unusual today's levels are.

P.title: wo-poles.c8.text
World: As Arctic sea ice shrinks, routes along the top of Russia and through Canada's islands stay open longer each summer. They can cut the sea journey between Europe and East Asia by about a third.\n\nTraffic is still small, because ice, darkness, storms and a lack of ports make them risky and costly.

P.title: wo-poles.c9.text
World: Sea level is rising for two main reasons: warmer water takes up more space, and ice on land is melting into the ocean. Greenland and Antarctica are losing hundreds of billions of tonnes of ice a year.\n\nThe rise is speeding up, threatening low coasts, including stretches of Portugal's.

P.title: wo-africa.summary
World: A huge, young and diverse continent.

P.title: wo-africa.q0.q
World: Which is Africa's most populous country?

P.title: wo-africa.q1.q
World: What is Africa's median age, approximately?

P.title: wo-africa.q2.q
World: In how many African countries is Portuguese official?

P.title: wo-africa.q2.x
World: Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe.

P.title: wo-africa.c0.text
World: Common world maps shrink Africa. It's bigger than the USA, China, India and most of Europe combined, at about 30 million km².

P.title: wo-africa.c1.text
World: Africa has 54 UN member states. Nigeria is the most populous (over 220 million), Algeria the largest by area.

P.title: wo-africa.c2.text
World: Africa's median age is about 19, compared with about 44 in Europe. By 2050, roughly a quarter of the world's people may live in Africa.

P.title: wo-africa.c3.text
World: Over 2,000 languages are spoken in Africa. Arabic, Swahili, Hausa, Amharic and Yoruba each have tens of millions of speakers. Portuguese is official in five countries.

P.title: wo-africa.c4.text
World: Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau and São Tomé and Príncipe make up the PALOP. Luanda and Maputo are big, fast-growing cities.

P.title: wo-africa.c5.text
World: The Sahara desert, the Nile, Mount Kilimanjaro, Victoria Falls, the Serengeti's migrations and the Okavango Delta are among the world's great natural sights.

P.title: wo-africa.c6.text
World: Africa holds large shares of the world's cobalt, platinum, diamonds, cocoa and many other resources. Turning them into broad prosperity remains a challenge.

P.title: wo-africa.c7.text
World: Africa leapt ahead with mobile money: Kenya's M-Pesa, launched in 2007, lets millions pay, save and send money by phone without a bank account.

P.title: wo-africa.c7.viz.steps.2
World: Pay and send money by SMS

P.title: wo-africa.c8.text
World: Africa is where humans evolved. Fossils such as "Lucy" (3.2 million years old, Ethiopia) and the oldest Homo sapiens remains (about 300,000 years, Morocco) were found there.

P.title: wo-africa.c9.text
World: Many African economies are among the world's fastest growing, with booming tech hubs in Lagos, Nairobi and Kigali. Challenges include poverty, conflict in some regions and climate risks.

P.title: wo-asia.summary
World: The largest continent, home to most of humanity.

P.title: wo-asia.q0.q
World: Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan?

P.title: wo-asia.q1.q
World: Until when was Macau administered by Portugal?

P.title: wo-asia.q2.q
World: Roughly what share of humanity lives in Asia?

P.title: wo-asia.c0.text
World: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land and holds nearly 60% of its people. It stretches from Turkey to Japan and from Siberia to Indonesia.

P.title: wo-asia.c1.text
World: Asia is usually split into East, South, Southeast, Central and West Asia (the Middle East), each with very different histories, religions and climates.

P.title: wo-asia.c1.viz.items.3
World: West and Central: Middle East, Kazakhstan

P.title: wo-asia.c2.text
World: China has about 1.4 billion people, the world's second-largest economy and a history of continuous civilisation over 3,500 years. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers of any language.

P.title: wo-asia.c3.text
World: India is the world's most populous country and largest democracy, with 22 scheduled languages and a booming technology sector. Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism were born on the subcontinent.

P.title: wo-asia.c4.text
World: Japan blends ancient traditions with advanced technology. Its population is shrinking and ageing fast; nearly 30% of people are over 65.

P.title: wo-asia.c5.text
World: Portuguese traders left words and places across Asia: "pão" became "pan" in Japanese, tempura has Portuguese roots, Macau was Portuguese until 1999, and Kristang creole is still spoken in Malacca.

P.title: wo-asia.c6.text
World: West Asia holds about half of the world's proven oil reserves and the holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam in Jerusalem, Mecca and Medina.

P.title: wo-asia.c6.viz.items.0
World: About half of world oil reserves

P.title: wo-asia.c7.text
World: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong grew from poverty to wealth in a few decades through exports, education and technology. Today Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced chips.

P.title: wo-asia.c8.text
World: Asia has the Himalaya, the Gobi desert, the Siberian taiga and great rivers like the Yangtze, Ganges, Mekong and Indus, which feed hundreds of millions of people.

P.title: wo-asia.c9.text
World: Many of the world's largest cities are in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Mumbai, Beijing and others with populations over 20 million in their urban areas.

P.title: wo-americas.summary
World: Two continents from the Arctic to Cape Horn.

P.title: wo-americas.q0.x
World: Cabral, on his way to India.

P.title: wo-americas.q1.q
World: Which country is second largest by area?

P.title: wo-americas.q2.q
World: Which foods came from the Americas?

P.title: wo-americas.c0.text
World: The Americas stretch about 14,000 km from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. North America includes Canada, the USA and Mexico; Central America links to South America at Panama.

P.title: wo-americas.c1.text
World: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago. Great civilisations followed: the Maya, the Aztecs with their capital Tenochtitlan, and the Inca empire in the Andes.

P.title: wo-americas.c2.text
World: After 1492, Spanish and Portuguese colonisation, followed by English, French and Dutch, transformed the Americas. Disease, war and forced labour killed a huge share of the native population.

P.title: wo-americas.c3.text
World: Brazil is the largest country in South America, with about 215 million people, the Amazon rainforest and the largest Portuguese-speaking population in the world.

P.title: wo-americas.c4.text
World: The USA is the world's largest economy, with 50 states and about 340 million people. Its culture, technology and companies have global influence.

P.title: wo-americas.c5.text
World: Canada is the world's second-largest country by area but has only about 40 million people, mostly living near the US border. English and French are official languages.

P.title: wo-americas.c6.text
World: Spanish is spoken from Mexico to Argentina; Portuguese in Brazil. Spanish speakers in the Americas outnumber those in Spain by about ten to one.

P.title: wo-americas.c7.text
World: The Andes are the world's longest mountain range on land, about 7,000 km. To their east, the Amazon basin holds the largest rainforest on Earth.

P.title: wo-americas.c8.text
World: Opened in 1914, the canal lets ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific without going around South America, saving about 13,000 km.

P.title: wo-americas.c8.viz.items.2.l
World: saved on a New York–San Francisco voyage

P.title: wo-americas.c9.text
World: The Americas gave the world maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cocoa, vanilla, peanuts and turkeys. Imagine Portuguese food without potatoes and tomatoes!

P.title: wo-oceania.summary
World: Islands, Australia and the frozen ends of the Earth.

P.title: wo-oceania.q0.q
World: How long have Aboriginal Australians lived in Australia?

P.title: wo-oceania.q0.x
World: One of the oldest continuous cultures.

P.title: wo-oceania.q1.q
World: Which was the first country to give women the vote, in 1893?

P.title: wo-oceania.q2.o1
World: An ocean covered by sea ice

P.title: wo-oceania.c0.text
World: Oceania includes Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and thousands of Pacific islands grouped as Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.

P.title: wo-oceania.c1.text
World: Australia is both a country and a continent, mostly dry outback with most people living on the coast. It's home to unique animals like kangaroos, koalas and platypuses.

P.title: wo-oceania.c1.viz.items.2.l
World: live within 50 km of the coast

P.title: wo-oceania.c2.text
World: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

P.title: wo-oceania.c3.text
World: Off northeast Australia, the Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 km, the largest structure built by living things. Warming seas cause coral bleaching.

P.title: wo-oceania.c4.text
World: New Zealand's two main islands have volcanoes, glaciers and fjords. The Māori arrived around 1300 CE, among the last large lands settled by humans.

P.title: wo-oceania.c4.viz.events.3.l
World: first country to give women the vote

P.title: wo-oceania.c5.text
World: Polynesians crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, reaching Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand.

P.title: wo-oceania.c6.text
World: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, mostly covered by floating sea ice. It's warming about three to four times faster than the global average, shrinking summer ice.

P.title: wo-oceania.c7.text
World: Above the Arctic Circle, the Sun never sets around the summer solstice and never rises around the winter solstice. At the poles themselves, there are six months of day and six of night.

P.title: wo-oceania.c8.text
World: Inuit, Sámi and other Arctic peoples have adapted to extreme cold for thousands of years. Animals use fat, fur and migration; Antarctic fish have antifreeze proteins in their blood.

P.title: wo-oceania.c9.text
World: Low-lying Pacific nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati are only a few metres above sea level and are among the most threatened by rising seas.

P.title: wo-economy.title
World: How the world earns a living

P.title: wo-economy.summary
World: GDP, trade and why some countries are richer.

P.title: wo-economy.q0.o1
World: The total value of goods and services produced

P.title: wo-economy.q1.q
World: What does the ECB usually do to fight high inflation?

P.title: wo-economy.q2.q
World: What share of Portugal's economy is services?

P.title: wo-economy.c0.text
World: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. It measures the size of an economy, not how well off people are.

P.title: wo-economy.c1.text
World: The USA is the largest economy, followed by China, Germany, Japan and India. Measured by purchasing power, China is the largest.

P.title: wo-economy.c2.text
World: Dividing GDP by population gives a better sense of average income. Luxembourg, Ireland and Switzerland rank high; Portugal is mid-table in the EU.

P.title: wo-economy.c3.text
World: Economies have three broad sectors: primary (farming, mining), secondary (industry) and tertiary (services). Rich countries are mostly services; Portugal's tourism is a major service export.

P.title: wo-economy.c4.text
World: Countries specialise in what they do relatively well and trade. Portugal exports cars, machinery, fuels, clothing, cork, wine and tourism, mainly to Spain, France and Germany.

P.title: wo-economy.c5.text
World: Inflation is a general rise in prices. The European Central Bank aims for about 2% a year. In 2022 inflation spiked across Europe with energy prices.

P.title: wo-economy.c6.text
World: Central banks raise interest rates to cool inflation and lower them to encourage borrowing and growth. Mortgage payments in Portugal, mostly variable-rate, follow the Euribor.

P.title: wo-economy.c7.text
World: Prices rise when demand outstrips supply, and fall when supply exceeds demand. Commodity markets, like wheat or soybeans, react quickly to harvests, weather and wars.

P.title: wo-economy.c8.text
World: Economists point to institutions (rule of law, low corruption), education, infrastructure, technology, trade openness and stability. Natural resources alone don't guarantee wealth.

P.title: wo-economy.c9.text
World: The Gini index measures inequality from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything). Nordic countries have low inequality; South Africa and Brazil high. Portugal is around the EU average.

P.title: wo-food.summary
World: Crops, commodities and how food travels.

P.title: wo-food.q0.q
World: Most soybean meal is used for…

P.title: wo-food.q1.q
World: What does a futures contract do?

P.title: wo-food.q1.o1
World: Fixes a price today for later delivery

P.title: wo-food.q2.q
World: Roughly how much food is lost or wasted?

P.title: wo-food.c0.text
World: Just a few crops supply most of humanity's calories: maize, rice, wheat and soybeans, plus sugar cane and palm oil.

P.title: wo-food.c1.text
World: The USA, China and Brazil lead maize; China and India rice; China, India and Russia wheat; Brazil and the USA soybeans. Weather in a few regions can move world prices.

P.title: wo-food.c2.text
World: About three-quarters of soybeans are crushed into meal for animal feed (chickens, pigs, fish), with the oil used for cooking and biodiesel.

P.title: wo-food.c3.text
World: Global traders buy grain and oilseeds from farmers, store them, ship them and sell them to millers, crushers and food companies worldwide, managing price, quality and logistics risks.

P.title: wo-food.c4.text
World: Futures contracts fix a price today for delivery later. Farmers and traders use them to hedge price risk. The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) sets benchmark prices for corn, soybeans and wheat.

P.title: wo-food.c4.viz.l.items.0
World: exposed if prices fall or rise

P.title: wo-food.c5.text
World: Grain moves on bulk carriers through key chokepoints: the Panama Canal, the Black Sea, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Malacca. Disruptions raise freight costs and prices.

P.title: wo-food.c6.text
World: Coffee grows mostly in Brazil, Vietnam and Colombia; cocoa mainly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Both are traded worldwide and sensitive to weather and plant disease.

P.title: wo-food.c7.text
World: Roughly a third of food produced is lost or wasted, from field to fridge. Reducing waste is one of the easiest ways to feed more people with less land and emissions.

P.title: wo-food.c7.viz.items.0.l
World: of food lost or wasted (FAO estimate)

P.title: wo-food.c8.text
World: Modern yields depend on fertilisers. Nitrogen fertiliser made with the Haber–Bosch process feeds roughly half the world's population, but uses natural gas and causes pollution if overused.

P.title: wo-food.c9.text
World: Portugal imports most of its cereals but exports wine, olive oil, tomatoes, fruit and cork. Olive groves in the Alentejo have expanded hugely thanks to Alqueva irrigation.

P.title: wo-energy.summary
World: How the world powers itself, and how that's changing.

P.title: wo-energy.q0.q
World: About how much of world primary energy still comes from fossil fuels?

P.title: wo-energy.q0.x
World: Oil, coal and gas still dominate.

P.title: wo-energy.q1.q
World: When did Portugal stop burning coal for power?

P.title: wo-energy.q2.q
World: What is green hydrogen made with?

P.title: wo-energy.c0.text
World: Fossil fuels (oil, coal, gas) still supply about 80% of the world's primary energy. Renewables and nuclear make up the rest, growing quickly in electricity.

P.title: wo-energy.c1.text
World: Electricity is only about 20% of final energy use. Transport, heating and industry still burn fuels directly, which is why electrifying them matters.

P.title: wo-energy.c2.text
World: Solar power has become the cheapest electricity in history in many places. Global solar capacity grew more than tenfold in a decade.

P.title: wo-energy.c2.viz.events.2.l
World: cheapest new power in many places

P.title: wo-energy.c3.text
World: Oil fuels most transport. The biggest producers are the USA, Saudi Arabia and Russia. OPEC+ coordinates production to influence prices.

P.title: wo-energy.c4.text
World: Europe imported much of its gas from Russia until 2022. After the invasion of Ukraine, it switched to LNG from the USA, Qatar and others. Portugal's Sines terminal receives LNG.

P.title: wo-energy.c5.text
World: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fuel. China burns over half the world's coal. Portugal closed its last coal power plants in 2021.

P.title: wo-energy.c5.viz.items.1.l
World: of world coal burned in China

P.title: wo-energy.c6.text
World: Energy use per person varies hugely: an average American uses several times more than an average Portuguese and dozens of times more than someone in many African countries.

P.title: wo-energy.c6.viz.unit
World: kWh per person per year (primary, approx.)

P.title: wo-energy.c7.text
World: Green hydrogen, made by splitting water with renewable electricity, could fuel steelmaking, fertiliser and shipping. Portugal is planning projects, notably around Sines.

P.title: wo-energy.c8.text
World: Countries want energy that's affordable, reliable and not dependent on a single supplier. Renewables, storage, interconnections and efficiency improve security.

P.title: wo-energy.c9.text
World: The world is shifting from fossil fuels to clean electricity, but the transition requires huge investment in grids, storage, minerals and new industries.

P.title: wo-water.summary
World: A precious and unevenly shared resource.

P.title: wo-water.q0.q
World: Which sector uses most fresh water?

P.title: wo-water.q1.q
World: Which agreement manages rivers shared by Portugal and Spain?

P.title: wo-water.q2.x
World: High pressure pushes water through membranes.

P.title: wo-water.c0.text
World: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or deep underground. Rivers and lakes hold a tiny fraction.

P.title: wo-water.c1.text
World: The Sun evaporates water from oceans and land; it condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back via rivers and groundwater. The cycle never stops.

P.title: wo-water.c2.text
World: Agriculture accounts for about 70% of fresh water withdrawals worldwide. Drip irrigation, used widely in the Alentejo, can cut water use dramatically.

P.title: wo-water.c3.text
World: Producing goods uses water. A cup of coffee takes about 140 litres along the supply chain; a kilo of beef around 15,000 litres.

P.title: wo-water.c4.text
World: About 2 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, and many more lack safe sanitation, mostly in rural areas of Africa and Asia.

P.title: wo-water.c5.text
World: Southern Portugal and Spain face more frequent droughts. Reservoirs like Alqueva, desalination plans in the Algarve and water reuse help, along with careful farming.

P.title: wo-water.c6.text
World: Desalination removes salt from seawater, mostly by reverse osmosis. It's reliable but energy-intensive. Countries like Israel and Saudi Arabia rely heavily on it.

P.title: wo-water.c7.text
World: Many rivers cross borders. Portugal and Spain manage their shared rivers under the 1998 Albufeira Convention, which sets minimum flows Spain must let through.

P.title: wo-water.c8.text
World: Aquifers store water underground. Pumping faster than rain refills them lowers water tables and can let seawater in near coasts.

P.title: wo-water.c9.text
World: Fixing leaks, efficient taps and showers, full loads in the dishwasher and washing machine, and collecting rainwater for the garden all cut use.

P.title: wo-orgs.q0.q
World: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?

P.title: wo-orgs.q1.q
World: Which Portuguese politician became UN Secretary-General in 2017?

P.title: wo-orgs.q1.x
World: He'd led the UN Refugee Agency.

P.title: wo-orgs.q2.o1
World: An attack on one is an attack on all

P.title: wo-orgs.c0.text
World: Founded in 1945, the UN has 193 member states. The General Assembly gives each one vote; the Security Council handles peace and security.

P.title: wo-orgs.c1.text
World: It has 15 members: five permanent ones with veto power (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and ten elected for two years. Portugal last served in 2011–12.

P.title: wo-orgs.c2.text
World: Former Portuguese prime minister António Guterres became UN Secretary-General in 2017, after leading the UN Refugee Agency. His second term runs to the end of 2026.

P.title: wo-orgs.c3.text
World: Specialised agencies work on health (WHO), food (FAO, WFP), children (UNICEF), refugees (UNHCR), culture (UNESCO) and more.

P.title: wo-orgs.c4.text
World: The European Commission proposes laws, the Parliament (elected) and Council (national governments) adopt them, and the Court of Justice interprets them.

P.title: wo-orgs.c5.text
World: NATO is a military alliance founded in 1949. An attack on one member is treated as an attack on all (Article 5). It has 32 members after Finland and Sweden joined in 2023–24.

P.title: wo-orgs.c6.text
World: The IMF lends to countries in crisis (including Portugal in 2011), the World Bank funds development, the WTO sets trade rules and the OECD compares policies among richer countries.

P.title: wo-orgs.c7.text
World: The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, founded in 1996, links nine countries where Portuguese is official, promoting the language and cooperation.

P.title: wo-orgs.c7.viz.items.4
World: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé, Timor-Leste, Equatorial Guinea

P.title: wo-orgs.c8.text
World: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states; the International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both sit in The Hague.

P.title: wo-orgs.c9.text
World: International organisations depend on members' willingness. Vetoes, unpaid budgets and rivalries limit what they can do, but they remain the main forums for global problems.

P.title: wo-cultures.summary
World: Beliefs, festivals and customs, in brief.

P.title: wo-cultures.q0.q
World: How many cheek kisses are usual in Portugal?

P.title: wo-cultures.q0.x
World: Two, starting with the right cheek.

P.title: wo-cultures.q1.q
World: Why does Ramadan move earlier each year?

P.title: wo-cultures.q1.o1
World: The Islamic calendar is lunar, about 11 days shorter

P.title: wo-cultures.q2.q
World: Which three religions consider Jerusalem sacred?

P.title: wo-cultures.c0.text
World: Christianity and Islam are the largest religions, followed by Hinduism and Buddhism. About 15% of people are unaffiliated with any religion.

P.title: wo-cultures.c1.text
World: Judaism, Christianity and Islam share roots in the figure of Abraham and belief in one God. Jerusalem is sacred to all three.

P.title: wo-cultures.c2.title
World: Religions of India and East Asia

P.title: wo-cultures.c2.text
World: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism began in South Asia. Confucianism, Taoism and Shinto shaped China and Japan, often blended with Buddhism.

P.title: wo-cultures.c3.text
World: Most Portuguese identify as Catholic, though regular practice has declined. Fátima, where Marian apparitions were reported in 1917, is one of the world's major pilgrimage sites.

P.title: wo-cultures.c4.text
World: Most of the world uses the Gregorian calendar (1582). The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year. Chinese New Year follows a lunisolar calendar.

P.title: wo-cultures.c5.text
World: Many cultures celebrate light in the dark season: Diwali (Hindu), Hanukkah (Jewish), Christmas (Christian) and Lunar New Year lanterns.

P.title: wo-cultures.c6.text
World: Customs differ: handshakes, bows in Japan, cheek kisses in Portugal and France (two kisses in Portugal), the wai in Thailand, namaste in India.

P.title: wo-cultures.c7.text
World: Attitudes to time vary: Swiss and German meetings start exactly on time; in many Mediterranean and Latin American cultures, schedules are more flexible. Knowing the norms avoids misunderstandings.

P.title: wo-cultures.c8.text
World: In low-context cultures (Germany, Netherlands, USA), people say things explicitly. In high-context cultures (Japan, China, Arab countries), much is implied by relationship and situation.

P.title: wo-cultures.c9.text
World: UNESCO lists over 1,200 World Heritage sites. Portugal has 17, including the Jerónimos Monastery, Sintra, the historic centres of Porto, Évora and Guimarães, and the Douro wine region.

P.title: wo-cities.q0.q
World: Since about when have more people lived in cities than in the countryside?

P.title: wo-cities.q1.o1
World: A city of over 10 million people

P.title: wo-cities.c0.text
World: Since about 2007, more people live in cities than in the countryside. By 2050 about two-thirds of humanity is expected to be urban.

P.title: wo-cities.c1.text
World: Cities with over 10 million people are megacities. There are over 30 today, most in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Mexico City, Cairo, Mumbai.

P.title: wo-cities.c2.text
World: Cities offer jobs, education, healthcare and opportunity. Clustering people and firms boosts productivity and innovation.

P.title: wo-cities.c3.text
World: Lisbon's metropolitan area has about 2.9 million people, Porto's about 1.8 million. Together they hold nearly half of Portugal's population.

P.title: wo-cities.c4.text
World: About a billion people live in slums or informal settlements without secure housing, clean water or sanitation, mostly in fast-growing cities of Africa and Asia.

P.title: wo-cities.c4.viz.items.0.l
World: people in slums or informal settlements (UN estimate)

P.title: wo-cities.c5.text
World: Good public transport, cycling and walking make cities more liveable. Lisbon's trams and metro, Porto's metro (opened 2002) and new bus rapid transit lines aim to reduce car dependence.

P.title: wo-cities.c6.text
World: The idea: everyday needs like shops, schools, health and parks should be reachable within 15 minutes on foot or by bike. Paris has promoted it since 2020.

P.title: wo-cities.c7.text
World: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat, making cities several degrees warmer than surrounding countryside. Trees, parks, light-coloured roofs and water features cool them.

P.title: wo-cities.c8.text
World: Many popular cities, including Lisbon and Porto, face rising rents and house prices driven by demand, tourism and limited supply. Governments try new construction, rent rules and limits on short-term rentals.

P.title: wo-cities.c9.text
World: Sensors and data help cities manage traffic lights, parking, waste collection, water leaks and air quality more efficiently.

P.title: wo-climatechange.summary
World: What's happening, why, and what can be done.

P.title: wo-climatechange.q0.q
World: What was the CO₂ concentration before industry?

P.title: wo-climatechange.q1.q
World: What does the Paris Agreement aim for?

P.title: wo-climatechange.q2.q
World: When does Portugal aim for climate neutrality?

P.title: wo-climatechange.c0.text
World: Greenhouse gases like CO₂ and methane let sunlight in but trap some of the heat Earth radiates. Without them Earth would be about −18 °C on average; with more of them, it warms.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c1.text
World: CO₂ in the air was about 280 parts per million before industry. It passed 420 ppm in 2023, the highest in at least 800,000 years.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c2.text
World: The world is about 1.2–1.3 °C warmer than pre-industrial times on average. 2024 was the warmest year on record, around 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial average.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c3.text
World: Most emissions come from burning fossil fuels for electricity and heat, transport, industry and buildings. Agriculture and land use (deforestation, livestock) add a large share.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c4.text
World: Warming brings more heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and heavy rain; rising seas; shrinking glaciers and sea ice; and stress on crops and ecosystems.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c5.text
World: Portugal is among Europe's most exposed countries: hotter summers, longer droughts in the south, more severe wildfires, and coastal erosion along the Atlantic.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c5.viz.items.1
World: Droughts in the Alentejo and Algarve

P.title: wo-climatechange.c6.text
World: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, almost every country agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C, aiming for 1.5 °C, with national plans updated every five years.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c7.text
World: Net zero means cutting emissions as close to zero as possible and balancing the rest with removals (forests, carbon capture). Portugal aims for climate neutrality by 2045.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c8.text
World: The biggest levers: clean electricity, electrified transport and heating, efficient buildings and industry, protecting forests, less food waste and changes in diet.

P.title: wo-climatechange.c9.text
World: Even with cuts, some change is locked in. Adaptation means preparing: heat plans, fire-resistant landscapes, water storage, flood defences and resilient crops.

P.title: wo-hazards.summary
World: Earthquakes, volcanoes, storms and how to prepare.

P.title: wo-hazards.q0.q
World: How much more energy does a magnitude 7 release than a magnitude 5?

P.title: wo-hazards.q1.q
World: What should you do during an earthquake?

P.title: wo-hazards.q1.x
World: Then move to high ground near the coast after strong shaking.

P.title: wo-hazards.q2.q
World: A hurricane in the northwest Pacific is called a…

P.title: wo-hazards.c0.text
World: Earthquakes happen when stress along a fault is suddenly released. Most occur at plate boundaries. Portugal sits near the boundary between the Eurasian and African plates.

P.title: wo-hazards.c1.text
World: Magnitude scales are logarithmic: each whole step releases about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 8 releases about 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 6.

P.title: wo-hazards.c2.title
World: What to do in an earthquake

P.title: wo-hazards.c2.text
World: Drop, cover and hold on: get under a sturdy table, protect your head and hold on until shaking stops. Stay away from windows. Near the coast, move to high ground if shaking is strong or long.

P.title: wo-hazards.c2.viz.steps.3
World: After shaking: coast? Go to high ground

P.title: wo-hazards.c3.text
World: Undersea earthquakes can lift the sea floor and launch tsunamis that cross oceans at jet speed. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people.

P.title: wo-hazards.c4.text
World: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, at plate boundaries or hotspots. The Azores have active volcanoes; Capelinhos on Faial erupted in 1957–58, adding new land.

P.title: wo-hazards.c5.text
World: Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans (above about 26.5 °C). They're called hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the northwest Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

P.title: wo-hazards.c6.text
World: Hot, dry, windy weather plus fuel (dense undergrowth, eucalyptus and pine plantations) makes fires spread fast. In 2017, wildfires in Portugal killed over 100 people.

P.title: wo-hazards.c7.text
World: Floods come from heavy rain, rivers overflowing, storm surges and flash floods in steep valleys. Building on flood plains increases the damage.

P.title: wo-hazards.c8.text
World: Heatwaves are the deadliest weather hazard in Europe, especially for older people. Drink water, stay cool, check on vulnerable neighbours and avoid the midday sun.

P.title: wo-hazards.c8.viz.items.4
World: Never leave anyone in a parked car

P.title: wo-hazards.c9.text
World: Know your local risks, have an emergency kit (water, torch, radio, medicines, documents), agree a family meeting point and follow official alerts from Proteção Civil.
